newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST-Bearish distillate build seen in API data.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-Bearish distillate build seen in API data.

text.p: An already jittery oil market could slide following Tuesday evening's inventory report by the American Petroleum Institute which is expected to show a bearish build in historically low heating oil stocks.
"If there is a bearish report, then it will have more of an impact than a bullish report would," said William Brown, a trader and president of W.H. Brown & Co.
A Reuters survey forecasts total distillates, which includes heating oil, to build 1.8 million barrels. Trader estimates ranged between up 500,000 to three million barrels.

Exports to Europe, where heating oil is also in tight supply, are expected to decrease after a rush on cargoes the previous week to European Union countries before new distillate specifications became effective.
"The exports were supposedly done in a hurry before the specifications, so they should now be tapering off," said Tim Evans, an analyst with Pegusus Econometric Group.

Traders said long anticipated imports of gasoline ended up not being as substantial as thought and refiners have shifted to distillates ahead of the winter, so gasoline stocks are expected to remain mostly stable.

Meanwhile, crude imports are expected to have declined and refinery operating rates are seen remaining near a feverish 95.5 percent, draining total crude stocks. The Reuters survey forecasts a draw of 1.5 million barrels, with estimates ranging from a draw of two million to a build of 1.5 million.

Despite an expected draw in crude, the spectre of Iraqi oil returning to the market reappeared Tuesday morning. Iraq's Foreign Minister Mohammed Saeed al-Sahaf said he saw a consensus among foreign ministers at a UN General Assembly meeting in New York for a speedy implementation of the oil-for food deal.

Under the deal, trade sanctions imposed on Iraq over its 1990 invasion of Kuwait would be lifted by the United Nations and Iraq would be allowed to export $2 billion of oil in exchange for humanitarian aid.
"This is going to keep the longs nervous, so a bearish report will push down prices that much more," said ING Derivatives analyst Tom Bentz.
Traders said upside in the market is dependent on heating oil, which has hit post-Gulf War highs on stocks being 18 million barrels below a year ago.

Most of the deficit is in the northeastern United States, the world's largest market for heating oil. However, the U.S. Energy Information Administration said Monday there would be sufficient heating oil supplies to meet winter demand.
"I just feel heating oil (prices) has done what it can do for the time being," said W.H. Brown's William Brown.

Brown said the runup in heating oil prices already reflects a low inventory situation, so there would be little upside on bullish invnetory data, especially with speculation surrounding a return of Iraqi oil.
"There has been a change in psychology that reflects the returning spectre of Iraqi oil," said Brown.
